meta.title: Who really said "I'd put my money on the sun and solar energy. What a source of power! I hope we don't have to wait until oil and coal run out before we tackle that"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Edison's solar line appears only in James Newton's 1987 memoir, recalling a 1931 talk. No contemporaneous source, so we mark it attributed, not verified.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I'd put my money on the sun and solar energy. What a source of power! I hope we don't have to wait until oil and coal run out before we tackle that'?
meta.ogDescription: First printed in James Newton's 1987 memoir Uncommon Friends, recalling a 1931 talk with Ford and Firestone. Edison's view is real; this wording is remembered, not documented.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.sourceLine: Widely credited to Edison and squarely consistent with views he put in print in 1910 — but the sentence itself appears nowhere before James D. Newton’s 1987 memoir Uncommon Friends, which recalls a March 1931 conversation fifty-six years after the fact. Quote Investigator found no earlier instance and calls the reliability of Newton’s dialog uncertain ↗.

source.heading: Where the sentence actually comes from

docMeta.dd: Uncommon Friends: Life with Thomas Edison, Henry Ford, Harvey Firestone, Alexis Carrel & Charles Lindbergh
James D. Newton (1905–1999) · Harcourt Brace Jovanovich, San Diego, 1987 · p. 31
March 1931 — Edison with Henry Ford and Harvey Firestone, per Newton’s recollection; published fifty-six years later
Interview by Elbert Hubbard, “The Open Road: Afoot With The Fra,” The Fra: A Journal of Affirmation, vol. 5, no. 1 (April 1910), 6–7

source.excerpt: We are like tenant farmers, chopping down the fence around our house for fuel, when we should be using nature’s inexhaustible sources of energy—sun, wind, and tide. … I’d put my money on the sun and solar energy. What a source of power! I hope we don’t have to wait till oil and coal run out before we tackle that. I wish I had more years left!
trail: April 1910 — Edison, interviewed by Elbert Hubbard in The Fra: A Journal of Affirmation, says on the record that natural forces should supply our power and that someone will find a way of “concentrating and storing up sunshine.” Quote Investigator credits Edison with these statements ↗.
March 1931 — the date Newton assigns to the conversation with Ford and Firestone in which Edison reportedly spoke this line. Edison died on 18 October 1931.
1987 — the sentence appears in print for the first time, in Uncommon Friends (Harcourt Brace Jovanovich), p. 31. Read the book at the Internet Archive ↗.
2015 — Quote Investigator examines the quotation, finds no earlier attestation, and declines to vouch for the dialog’s reliability. Wikiquote likewise carries it only with the Newton citation ↗.
source.excerptNote: As reproduced by Quote Investigator ↗ from Newton’s book. In the surrounding dialog Firestone raises the depletion of oil and coal and wonders about harnessing wind, and Ford mentions the power of tides such as the Bay of Fundy, before Edison answers with these lines. Note “till” — the circulating version says “until.”

author.name: Thomas Edison
author.heading: Who was Thomas Edison?
author.bio: Thomas Alva Edison (born 11 February 1847, died 18 October 1931 in West Orange, New Jersey) was an American inventor and businessman who held 1,093 US patents, including work on the phonograph, the incandescent lamp and motion pictures. He was also a relentless talker to reporters, and his offhand predictions were printed, paraphrased and recycled for decades. That combination — enormous fame plus a huge volume of loosely recorded conversation — is exactly why lines like this one attach to him so easily, and why which record a quotation comes from matters more for Edison than for almost any other American figure.

copyAttribution: "I'd put my money on the sun and solar energy. What a source of power! I hope we don't have to wait till oil and coal run out before we tackle that." — Thomas Edison, in conversation with Henry Ford and Harvey Firestone, March 1931, as recalled in James D. Newton, Uncommon Friends (San Diego: Harcourt Brace Jovanovich, 1987), 31. Attributed, not verified: the memoir was published fifty-six years after the conversation and no contemporaneous source records the line. The widely circulated form substitutes "until" for Newton's "till."

misattribution.heading: What gets said about this quote that isn’t quite right
misattribution.intro: Nobody credits this line to the wrong person — Edison is the only claimant. What goes wrong is the confidence: the wording drifts, the date is presented as documented fact, and the passage is trimmed until it changes character.

items.why: Newton’s book reads “till oil and coal run out,” not “until.” The smoothed form is now overwhelmingly the one in circulation, including on Wikiquote. Quote Investigator quotes the book’s wording, with “till” ↗.

Energy and climate pieces routinely present this as a documented 1931 statement. It is a friend’s recollection first printed in 1987; no letter, transcript, notebook or newspaper of the period carries it. QI located no earlier instance and says the reliability of the dialog is uncertain ↗.

items.who: The dropped opening and closing lines
items.why: As printed, the passage opens with Edison’s “tenant farmers, chopping down the fence around our house for fuel” image and ends “I wish I had more years left!” Both are usually cut, which turns a wistful remark from the last year of his life into a clean technological forecast. The full passage as QI reproduces it ↗.

The 1931 line is often blended with, or used as a citation for, what Edison actually said on the record in April 1910 about sunshine, winds and tides. Those are two different sources with very different evidentiary weight. QI on the documented 1910 interview ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: Edison genuinely championed harnessing the sun, and said so in print in April 1910 — but this famous sentence rests on one friend’s recollection published in 1987, so quote it as attributed, not documented. See Quote Investigator on what Edison verifiably said ↗.

context.heading: Why this one keeps getting quoted
lead: This is the single most-cited piece of evidence that Thomas Edison “predicted solar power,” and it turns up in climate journalism, renewable-energy pitch decks and conference keynotes with a confident date attached: 1931, the last year of his life. The date comes from a memoir published in 1987 by James D. Newton, a younger friend of Edison, Ford and Firestone, who wrote that he had kept a diary recording “times and places, key phrases, and vivid impressions” across nearly fifty years.

The honest picture is layered. Edison really did argue, on the record and in print, that burning fuel was a waste and that the sun, wind and tide were the sensible sources — he said so to Elbert Hubbard in an interview published in The Fra in April 1910. What is not documented is this particular, much punchier sentence. It exists only as one friend’s recollection, printed fifty-six years after the conversation it describes.
context.detailsSummary: The two records, side by side
detailsBody: April 1910 — documented, in print. In an interview with Elbert Hubbard published in The Fra: A Journal of Affirmation, Edison said “We should utilize natural forces and thus get all of our power. Sunshine is a form of energy, and the winds and the tides are manifestations of energy,” and predicted that “some day some fellow will invent a way of concentrating and storing up sunshine.” Quote Investigator credits Edison for these statements ↗.

March 1931 — recalled, published 1987. Newton’s Uncommon Friends places the “money on the sun” exchange in a conversation with Ford and Firestone. Edison died on 18 October 1931, the same year; the passage ends “I wish I had more years left!” That closing line is almost always dropped when the quote is reproduced, which turns an old man’s wistful aside into a crisp technological forecast.
context.pull: Edison’s solar views are documented. This specific sentence is remembered.
